The Sea goldie, Pseudanthias squamipinnis, is a protogynous hermaphroditic serranid that forms large aggregations above Indo-Pacific coral reefs. Newly hatched yolk-sac larvae are remarkably small, with each prolarva emerging from an incubating egg approximately 0.8 millimeters in diameter, a size that yields a wet weight at birth of just 0.000268 grams [Wwb = 0.000268 grams]. This minute initial mass necessitates a rapid trophic switch following yolk-sac resorption, as the exotrophic transition must occur before endogenous reserves are exhausted. Growth trajectories derived from otolith increment analyses indicate that individuals can attain a total length of 15 centimeters [Li = 15 centimeters] under favorable conditions, although this ultimate size is rarely observed in the wild due to intense predation pressure. The species is characterized by strong sexual dimorphism in coloration, with males displaying vivid magenta and orange hues while females remain a more subdued orange-yellow, a pattern linked to their complex social hierarchy.

Sexual maturation in this species is closely tied to body size rather than chronological age, with female puberty occurring once individuals reach approximately 5 centimeters [Lp = approximately 5 centimeters] in total length. Below this threshold, juveniles are functionally immature and do not exhibit gonadal activity. The transition from female to male, which involves complete gonadal reorganization, typically begins at a total length of around 7 centimeters, a size at which individuals have already passed through puberty and are reproductively active as females. This sex change is socially mediated; removal of the dominant male from a harem triggers rapid behavioral and physiological transformation in the largest female. The wet weight at puberty for a typical female at the onset of maturity is estimated at 4 grams [Wwp = 4 grams], a mass that reflects the accumulation of somatic tissue necessary to support vitellogenesis and subsequent spawning.

Reproductive output in the Sea goldie is strongly influenced by ambient temperature, which modulates both gametogenic cycles and spawning frequency. In the laboratory at a stable water temperature of 27.6 °C [T = 27.6 °C], females of approximately 7 centimeters total length have been recorded producing, on average, 14,000 eggs per year . This figure represents a combined result of relatively small clutch sizes and high spawning frequency; individual females may spawn multiple times within a single reproductive season, releasing batches of pelagic eggs into the water column during dusk hours. The eggs are transparent and buoyant, drifting with planktonic currents for several days before hatching. The annual reproductive output of nearly 14,000 eggs underscores the species' strategy of high fecundity offset by low per-offspring investment, a common pattern among small-bodied coral reef teleosts.

The ultimate wet weight attained by adult Sea goldies is approximately 74.4 grams [Wwi = approximately 74.4 grams], a mass that is typically reached only by the largest terminal-phase males that have held dominant positions within a harem for extended periods. Females, which remain smaller on average, rarely exceed 30 grams due to the social suppression of growth and the energetic demands of repeated spawning events. The length-weight relationship follows a power function consistent with other members of the subfamily Anthiinae, with the asymptotic mass reflecting the maximum size achievable under natural reef conditions. This body size constraint has direct implications for reproductive success, as larger males are better able to defend spawning territories and mate with multiple females. Intraspecific variation in ultimate mass is therefore tied not only to genetic factors but also to social rank and local resource availability across different reef habitats.

Longevity in the Sea goldie is moderate for a small reef fish, with maximum recorded lifespan in the wild estimated at 10 years [am = 10 years] when maintained at an average water temperature of approximately 27.6 °C [T = 27.6 °C]. This figure is derived from mark-recapture studies and validated by otolith age-reading techniques. The relationship between lifespan and temperature is consistent with the metabolic theory of ecology, as individuals inhabiting cooler waters may exhibit slightly slower aging rates. Post-reproductive senescence is not pronounced in this species; individuals typically maintain reproductive function until late in life, although spawning frequency may decline in the oldest females. The 10-year maximum lifespan places Pseudanthias squamipinnis among the longer-lived members of its genus, a trait that may be evolutionarily linked to its haremic social structure and the need for stable dominance hierarchies.
